title: How To Make Teaching (And Learning) Online Easier And Less Stressful easier-and-less-stressful/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In this article aimed at teachers newly thrust into online instruction, Linsin lays out eight strategies for reducing the stress of learning new platforms quickly. He begins with acceptance, arguing that resisting the shift only compounds stress, and encourages a curious, puzzle-solving mindset toward technical problems. Other tips include taking a slow, deliberate approach modeled on the Navy SEAL maxim 'slow is smooth, smooth is fast,' experimenting freely without publishing, favoring informal tutorials from real teachers over dense official documentation, and searching broad-to-narrow when researching a platform. He also urges teachers to use only the features they need rather than every available option, and to accept mistakes as an inevitable, even valuable, part of learning in front of students. The piece closes by recommending a written online classroom management plan regardless of platform.
points: Opens with acceptance as the first step, arguing that resisting the shift to online teaching only increases stress.
Recommends approaching new platforms with curiosity, treating technical problems as puzzles to solve rather than threats.
Advises favoring short, informal tutorials from real teachers over dense official platform documentation.
Suggests using only the few features you actually need rather than trying to master an entire platform at once.
Frames mistakes made in front of students as valuable and inevitable rather than something to fear.
quotes: So what follows are eight strategies to help you become comfortable teaching (and learning) online quickly and start enjoying the process rather than dreading it.
As soon as this decision is made, your stress level will drop and you’ll begin making real progress. You may even start enjoying the feeling of satisfaction that comes with acquiring new skills.
The Navy SEALs have a saying: Slow is smooth and smooth is fast.
Tutorials from real people are often far better and easier to understand. They tend to get to the meat of what you need to learn rather than pulling you down into the weeds.
View mistakes as inevitable and part of the process. They’re opportunities to learn at a deeper level. They add to your knowledge and let students know that it’s okay to mess up.
It’s the difference between an attentive, well-behaved class. And total chaos.
